title: Signs you can touch
hookLine: Catholics and Orthodox count seven sacraments; most Protestants two ordinances; Quakers keep them inwardly

lines: A RING, A HANDSHAKE, A HUG.
cards: A ring slid onto a finger. A hand on a shoulder at a funeral. A handshake that closes a deal.
A hug at the airport. None of them needs a word. People are bodies, and the deepest things they mean, they tend to say with hands, with objects, with water and bread and touch.
Christianity is full of this. Water poured over a baby's head. Bread broken and shared.
Oil smoothed on a sick person's forehead. Hands laid on someone being sent out. For many Christians these are not just symbols.

teach.b: Sacrament comes from the Latin sacramentum, and before the church used it, it meant a soldier's oath of loyalty, something sacred that binds you.
Early Latin Christians used it to translate a Greek word, mysterion, mystery; Orthodox Christians still call the sacraments the holy mysteries.
A classic definition, from the Anglican Book of Common Prayer: a sacrament is "an outward and visible sign of an inward and spiritual grace." Outward and visible: water, bread, wine, oil.
Inward and spiritual: what God gives through them. The churches count differently.

Catholics count seven, and Orthodox Christians usually name the same seven: baptism; confirmation, which Orthodox call chrismation; the Eucharist; confession; anointing of the sick; marriage; and ordination.
Most Protestant churches name two, baptism and the Lord's Supper, because Jesus commanded those two directly.

Many Baptists and others prefer the word ordinance: something ordered by Christ, done in obedience and remembrance. Anglicans and Lutherans hold the two as sacraments and treat the others as sacred rites.
A few, like Quakers and the Salvation Army, keep no outward sacraments at all.

Not because they don't care, but because they believe the reality should be lived inwardly and in every ordinary moment, not in a few set rites. Churches disagree about this in earnest, and each has reasons.
What they share is the conviction that God isn't only up in the clouds.

teach.h: GOD COMES CLOSE THROUGH ORDINARY THINGS.
teach.b: God comes close through water on skin, bread in a hand, a word spoken over you.
Grace, for many Christians, comes wrapped in the most ordinary things.

how: Catholic and Orthodox Christians celebrate seven sacraments across life, from baptism to anointing of the sick; most Protestant churches celebrate baptism and the Lord's Supper; Quakers and the Salvation Army keep no outward sacraments.

o: any church service held on a Sunday morning
a hymn sung at the end of a funeral
an outward sign of an inward grace from God

games.q: you're an early Latin-speaking Christian looking for a word for baptism and the Lord's Supper. you pick sacramentum. what did it mean before?
games.why: a sacred oath that bound a soldier. Christians used it to translate mysterion, mystery, which Orthodox Christians still say.

practice: Think of the ordinary things you'll touch today: water from the tap or in a glass, bread or whatever your bread is, lotion or oil on your hands, the hand of someone you love.
Pick one and imagine it carrying more than it seems to: care, welcome, life. If you pray, give thanks for it; if you don't, just let it be more than ordinary for a minute.

wordCard.voice: Sacrament. From the Latin for a sacred oath. An outward sign of inward grace: water, bread, oil, hands.
